# Basics of Machine Learning — Section 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

> [!NOTE]
> **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024 Scheme — GNEST305, Module 1):**
> The student is expected to understand the *foundational taxonomy* of Machine Learning, distinguish between the major learning paradigms, identify the components of a typical ML pipeline, and recognize the standard terminology (features, labels, model, training, inference).

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Machine Learning (ML)** is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI) that enables computer systems to **learn patterns from data** and **improve their performance on a specific task** over time **without being explicitly programmed** for every possible scenario.

In the formal KTU/AI literature, this is often attributed to **Arthur Samuel (1959)**, who defined ML as:

> *"The field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed."*

A more modern, mathematically rigorous definition by **Tom Mitchell (1997)** is:

> *"A computer program is said to learn from experience **E** with respect to some class of tasks **T** and performance measure **P**, if its performance at tasks in **T**, as measured by **P**, improves with experience **E**."*

The triplet $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{P}, \mathbf{E})$ is the **learning problem definition** and is fundamental to framing any ML problem in the KTU examination context.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — Learning Like a Toddler

Imagine you are teaching a small child to recognize a **cat** versus a **dog**:

- You don't write down *rules* like "if ear_shape = pointy AND whiskers = long AND sound = meow, then class = cat."
- Instead, you **show the child many examples** ("This is a cat. This is a dog. This is a cat...").
- The child gradually builds an **internal mental model** that maps visual features to the correct animal.

Machine Learning works **exactly the same way**:

- The *examples* are the **dataset**.
- The *features* (whiskers, ear shape, sound) are the **input variables** $X$.
- The *category* (cat/dog) is the **label** $y$.
- The *mental model* is the **learned function** $f_\theta(X) \approx y$.
- The act of refining the model by seeing more examples is **training**.

## 1.3 Core Building Blocks of an ML System

The standard KTU-mandated vocabulary for an ML problem includes the following:

| Symbol / Term | Meaning | Intuition |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbf{X}$ | Feature matrix (input) | The "clues" the model sees |
| $\mathbf{y}$ | Label / target vector (output) | The "answer" the model should predict |
| $f_\theta(\cdot)$ | Hypothesis / model with parameters $\theta$ | The "decision rule" being learned |
| $\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$ | Dataset of $N$ samples | The "textbook" the model studies |
| $\mathcal{L}(\hat{y}, y)$ | Loss function | The "penalty" for being wrong |
| Training | Minimizing $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathcal{D}$ | The "studying" phase |
| Inference / Prediction | Using $f_\theta$ on new, unseen data | The "exam" phase |
| Generalization | Performing well on *unseen* data | The "real-world test" |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Insight:** The single most important goal in ML is **generalization** — not memorization. A model that memorizes the training data is *overfit* and useless in practice.

## 1.4 Why Machine Learning Matters in Modern Engineering

> [!NOTE]
> ML is no longer optional — it sits at the core of:
> - **Recommendation systems** (Netflix, Amazon, Spotify)
> - **Computer vision** (medical imaging, autonomous vehicles)
> - **Natural Language Processing** (chatbots, translation, search)
> - **Predictive analytics** (weather, finance, energy grids)
> - **Anomaly detection** (cybersecurity, industrial fault diagnosis)

For KTU 2024 graduates, ML literacy is a baseline expectation across nearly all engineering disciplines.

# Basics of Machine Learning — Section 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Learning Problem (Mitchell's Formalism)

Given:

- **Task** $\mathbf{T}$: e.g., classify an email as spam / not-spam
- **Experience** $\mathbf{E}$: a dataset of past labeled emails
- **Performance** $\mathbf{P}$: e.g., accuracy, F1-score

The ML algorithm searches a **hypothesis space** $\mathcal{H}$ for a function $h^* \in \mathcal{H}$ that best maps inputs to outputs:

$$h^* = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \; \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \mathcal{D}} \big[\, \mathcal{L}\big(h(x),\, y\big) \big]$$

The expectation $\mathbb{E}[\cdot]$ is taken over the **true (unknown) data distribution** $\mathcal{D}$ — this is the **generalization risk**.

In practice, we do not know $\mathcal{D}$, so we approximate it using the **empirical risk** on the training set $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$:

$$\hat{h} = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{L}\big(h(x_i),\, y_i\big)$$

This is the **Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM)** principle — the theoretical backbone of supervised ML.

## 2.2 Taxonomy of Machine Learning (High-Yield for KTU)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Module 1 demands a clear understanding of the four primary learning paradigms.** Examiners frequently ask 3-mark and 14-mark questions on this taxonomy.

### 2.2.1 Supervised Learning

- The dataset contains **input-output pairs** $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$.
- The model learns a mapping $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$.
- Two sub-tasks:
  - **Classification:** $y$ is discrete (e.g., spam / not-spam).
  - **Regression:** $y$ is continuous (e.g., house price).
- Examples: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, SVM, k-NN, Neural Networks.

### 2.2.2 Unsupervised Learning

- The dataset contains **only inputs** $\mathbf{x}_i$ — **no labels**.
- The model discovers **structure, clusters, or patterns** on its own.
- Common tasks:
  - **Clustering:** group similar points (e.g., K-Means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical).
  - **Dimensionality Reduction:** compress features (e.g., PCA, t-SNE, UMAP).
  - **Association Rule Mining:** discover co-occurrence (e.g., Apriori, FP-Growth).

### 2.2.3 Reinforcement Learning (RL)

- An **agent** interacts with an **environment**.
- At each step, the agent takes an **action** $a_t$, receives a **reward** $r_t$, and transitions to a new **state** $s_{t+1}$.
- The goal: learn a **policy** $\pi(a \mid s)$ that maximizes cumulative future reward:

$$G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{k} \, r_{t+k+1}$$

where $\gamma \in [0, 1)$ is the **discount factor** that prioritizes near-term rewards.

- Examples: AlphaGo, robotic locomotion, game-playing agents.

### 2.2.4 Semi-Supervised Learning

- A **small labeled** dataset + a **large unlabeled** dataset.
- Combines the strengths of both worlds; common when labeling is expensive (e.g., medical imaging).

## 2.3 The Standard ML Pipeline (KTU High-Yield)

A typical end-to-end ML project follows this sequence:

1. **Problem Definition** — frame the business/research question as an ML task.
2. **Data Collection** — gather raw data from databases, sensors, APIs, web scraping.
3. **Data Preprocessing** — handle missing values, outliers, duplicates.
4. **Feature Engineering** — create, transform, select features.
5. **Data Splitting** — divide into **Training**, **Validation**, and **Test** sets (typical ratio: 60/20/20 or 70/15/15).
6. **Model Selection** — choose an appropriate algorithm.
7. **Training** — fit the model by minimizing the loss function.
8. **Hyperparameter Tuning** — adjust learning rate, regularization, depth, etc.
9. **Evaluation** — measure performance on the held-out test set.
10. **Deployment & Monitoring** — serve predictions and track drift.

## 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> **These are the formulas most frequently tested in KTU 2024 End-Semester Examinations for GNEST305 Module 1.** Memorize the table — it is your safety net for the 14-mark question.

| Concept | Formula | Notes / Units |
|---|---|---|
| Empirical Risk | $\hat{R}(h) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{L}(h(x_i), y_i)$ | Unitless; averaged loss over $N$ samples |
| Mean Squared Error (MSE) | $\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$ | Unit = (target unit)$^2$ |
| Root Mean Squared Error | $\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}}$ | Same unit as target |
| Mean Absolute Error | $\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \vert y_i - \hat{y}_i \vert$ | Use $\vert$ carefully in tables (prefer $\vert \cdot \vert$ outside) |
| Accuracy | $\text{Acc} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$ | Range: $[0, 1]$ |
| Precision | $\text{Prec} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$ | "Of those predicted positive, how many correct?" |
| Recall (Sensitivity) | $\text{Rec} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$ | "Of actual positives, how many caught?" |
| F1-Score | $F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Prec} \cdot \text{Rec}}{\text{Prec} + \text{Rec}}$ | Harmonic mean; range $[0, 1]$ |
| RL Cumulative Reward | $G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{k} \, r_{t+k+1}$ | Discount factor $\gamma \in [0, 1)$ |
| Train/Test Split Ratio | $\text{Typical} = 70\% / 30\%$ or $80\% / 20\%$ | Validation carved out from training |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Pitfall — LaTeX in Tables:** When writing $\vert y_i - \hat{y}_i \vert$ inside a markdown table row, the vertical bar `\|` may be misinterpreted as a column separator. Use the LaTeX command `\vert` or wrap the equation inside a `$\dots$` math block placed *between* table rows (not inside), as demonstrated in the cheat sheet above.

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

| Engineering Domain | ML Application | Learning Type |
|---|---|---|
| Civil (Structural Health) | Crack detection from vibration sensors | Supervised (Classification) |
| Mechanical (Predictive Maintenance) | Remaining-useful-life of bearings | Supervised (Regression) |
| Electrical (Smart Grid) | Load forecasting | Supervised (Regression) |
| CS / IT (Cybersecurity) | Intrusion detection in network traffic | Semi-Supervised / Supervised |
| Biomedical (Diagnostics) | Tumor classification from MRI | Supervised (Deep Learning) |
| Retail (Recommendation) | "Customers who bought X also bought Y" | Unsupervised (Association) |
| Robotics (Locomotion) | Walking policy for quadruped | Reinforcement Learning |

## 2.6 The 'Why' Behind the 'How'

- **Why supervised learning needs labels:** The model requires ground-truth "answers" to compute the loss $\mathcal{L}$ and update parameters $\theta$ via gradient descent.
- **Why unsupervised learning exists:** In many real domains (genomics, anomaly detection, customer segmentation), labels are unavailable or too costly.
- **Why RL uses rewards and not labels:** Actions have *delayed consequences*; only a scalar reward signal is available, not a per-step target.
- **Why we split data:** To honestly measure generalization; training on the test set is academic fraud and a guaranteed KTU valuation penalty.

# Basics of Machine Learning — Section 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: From Empirical Risk to Gradient Descent

> [!NOTE]
> The following derivation is the **analytical heart** of nearly every ML model. Examiners often test it as a 7-mark sub-question in Part B of the ESE.

We want to find parameters $\theta$ that minimize the **empirical risk**:

$$\hat{R}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{L}\big(f_\theta(x_i),\, y_i\big)$$

**Step 1 — Expand the inner objective.**
Substitute the model $f_\theta(x)$ (for example, a linear model $f_\theta(x) = \theta^\top x$):

$$\hat{R}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \big(y_i - \theta^\top x_i\big)^2$$

This is the **Mean Squared Error (MSE)** loss.

**Step 2 — Compute the gradient with respect to $\theta$.**
Apply the chain rule. The derivative of $(y_i - \theta^\top x_i)^2$ with respect to $\theta$ is:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \big(y_i - \theta^\top x_i\big)^2 = 2 \big(y_i - \theta^\top x_i\big) \cdot \big(-x_i\big)$$

**Step 3 — Sum over all $N$ samples and divide by $N$:**

$$\nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta) = -\frac{2}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \big(y_i - \theta^\top x_i\big) \, x_i$$

**Step 4 — Update rule (Gradient Descent).**
Move $\theta$ in the direction opposite to the gradient, scaled by the **learning rate** $\eta > 0$:

$$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \hat{R}\big(\theta^{(t)}\big)$$

Substituting the gradient computed in Step 3:

$$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} + \frac{2\eta}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \big(y_i - {\theta^{(t)}}^\top x_i\big) \, x_i$$

**Step 5 — Convergence criterion.**
Stop iterating when one of the following holds:

- $\vert \vert \nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta^{(t)}) \vert \vert_2 < \epsilon$ for a small tolerance $\epsilon$ (e.g., $10^{-6}$).
- A maximum number of iterations $T_{\max}$ is reached.
- The validation loss fails to improve for $k$ consecutive epochs (**early stopping**).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Normal Equation (closed-form solution).** For linear regression, we can solve $\nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta) = 0$ directly, yielding:
> $$\theta^* = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$$
> This requires $X^\top X$ to be invertible, which fails when features are collinear — a classic KTU viva question.

## 3.2 Derivation: Confusion Matrix Metrics

For a binary classification problem with classes $\{+, -\}$, every prediction falls into one of four outcomes:

| | Predicted Positive | Predicted Negative |
|---|---|---|
| **Actual Positive** | True Positive (TP) | False Negative (FN) |
| **Actual Negative** | False Positive (FP) | True Negative (TN) |

**Step 1 — Accuracy.**
Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions out of all predictions:

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$$

**Step 2 — Precision.**
Among all samples the model *predicted* as positive, what fraction is *truly* positive?

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$$

**Step 3 — Recall (True Positive Rate).**
Among all samples that are *actually* positive, what fraction did the model *catch*?

$$\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

**Step 4 — F1-Score (harmonic mean of Precision and Recall).**
The F1-score penalizes extreme imbalances between precision and recall:

$$F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot \text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

**Step 5 — Worked Numerical Example.**
Suppose a spam classifier produces: $TP = 90$, $FP = 10$, $FN = 5$, $TN = 895$.

Compute each metric:

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{90 + 895}{90 + 895 + 10 + 5} = \frac{985}{1000} = 0.985$$

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{90}{90 + 10} = \frac{90}{100} = 0.90$$

$$\text{Recall} = \frac{90}{90 + 5} = \frac{90}{95} \approx 0.947$$

$$F_1 = \frac{2 \times 0.90 \times 0.947}{0.90 + 0.947} = \frac{1.7046}{1.847} \approx 0.923$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Interpretation for KTU answers:** A 98.5% accuracy looks great — but precision and recall reveal the model is missing 5 real spam emails. Always report **multiple metrics**, not just accuracy.

## 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Choosing the Right Learning Paradigm

The KTU 2024 examiner expects you to *justify* your choice of learning paradigm. Use this decision matrix:

| If your data has... | And your goal is... | Then use... | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Labels for every sample | Predict a discrete class | Supervised (Classification) | Email spam detection |
| Labels for every sample | Predict a continuous value | Supervised (Regression) | House price prediction |
| No labels | Discover groups | Unsupervised (Clustering) | Customer segmentation |
| No labels | Reduce feature count | Unsupervised (Dim. Reduction) | Visualizing high-D data |
| No labels | Find co-occurrence rules | Unsupervised (Association) | Market basket analysis |
| Few labels + many unlabeled | Leverage both | Semi-Supervised | Medical image classification |
| Sequential interaction with environment | Maximize long-term reward | Reinforcement Learning | Game AI, robotics |

```mermaid
    C --> C3[Association Rules]

    C1 --> C1B[DBSCAN]

    D --> D1[Model-Based RL]

```

## 4.2 Standard ML Pipeline (Block-Level Architecture Flow)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    stepA([Raw Data]) --> stepB[Data Collection]
    stepB --> stepC[Data Preprocessing]
    stepC --> stepD[Feature Engineering]
    stepD --> stepE[Train/Val/Test Split]
    stepE --> stepF[Model Training]
    stepF --> stepG{Hyperparameter Tuning}
    stepG --> stepH[Model Evaluation on Test Set]
    stepH --> stepI{Performance Acceptable?}
    stepI -- No --> stepG
    stepI -- Yes --> stepJ[Deployment and Monitoring]
    stepJ --> stepK([Predictions on New Data])
    stepK --> stepL[Feedback Loop and Retraining]
    stepL --> stepB
```

## 4.3 Supervised Learning Workflow (Input → Model → Output)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    in1([x1]) --> mat[Feature Matrix X]
    in2([x2]) --> mat
    in3([xn]) --> mat
    mat --> mod[f_theta: Learned Model]
    mod --> out1([y_hat = f_theta of x1])
    mod --> out2([y_hat = f_theta of x2])
    mod --> out3([y_hat = f_theta of xn])
    lbl([Label y]) --> loss[Loss Function L]
    out1 --> loss
    loss --> opt[Optimizer: Update theta]
    opt --> mod
```

## 4.4 Reinforcement Learning Agent–Environment Loop

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    env([Environment at State s_t]) --> obs[Observation]
    obs --> agent([Agent])
    agent --> act[Action a_t]
    act --> env
    env --> rew[Reward r_t+1]
    env --> nxt[Next State s_t+1]
    nxt --> obs
    rew --> agent
```

## 4.5 Bias–Variance Tradeoff (Conceptual Block Diagram)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Total Error] --> B[Bias^2]
    A --> C[Variance]
    A --> D[Irreducible Noise]

    B --> B1[High = Underfitting]
    B --> B2[Model too simple]

    C --> C1[High = Overfitting]
    C --> C2[Model too complex]

    D --> D1[Cannot be reduced by any model]
```

# Basics of Machine Learning — Section 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

> [!NOTE]
> **Mark Distribution as per KTU 2024 Scheme (ESE Pattern for GNEST305):**
> - **Part A:** 3-mark short-answer questions (answer in 3–4 sentences, with definitions).
> - **Part B:** 14-mark descriptive questions with internal choice (each part 7 marks × 2 sub-parts).

---

## 5.1 Part A — 3-Mark Questions

### Question 1
**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Paper Style]**
**Define Machine Learning. State any two applications of ML in real-world engineering domains.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
Machine Learning is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence that enables systems to learn patterns from data and improve their performance on a given task without being explicitly programmed (Mitchell, 1997). Two real-world applications are:
1. **Predictive maintenance** in mechanical engineering — using sensor data and supervised regression to predict the remaining useful life of bearings and motors.
2. **Medical image classification** in biomedical engineering — using deep convolutional networks to detect tumors in MRI scans.

*(1 mark for the definition, 1 mark for each application = 3 marks)*

---

### Question 2
**[KTU University Exam – June 2024, Model Paper Style]**
**Differentiate between Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning with one example each.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Paradigm | Data Requirement | Goal | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised | Labeled $(\mathbf{x}, y)$ pairs | Learn $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ | Email spam classification |
| Unsupervised | Unlabeled $\mathbf{x}$ only | Discover structure / clusters | Customer segmentation using K-Means |
| Reinforcement | Reward signal $r_t$ from environment | Maximize cumulative reward $G_t$ | AlphaGo learning to play Go |

*(1 mark per row = 3 marks)*

---

## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Questions (with Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**

**(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the four major types of Machine Learning paradigms in detail. For each, state the data requirement, the objective, and provide one engineering example.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Consider a binary classifier evaluated on a test set with the following counts: $TP = 80$, $FP = 20$, $FN = 30$, $TN = 870$. Compute the Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Score. Comment on whether accuracy alone is a reliable metric here.

---

#### Model Solution — Part A(a) [7 Marks]

**1. Supervised Learning** *(2 marks)*
- Data requirement: a dataset of labeled examples $\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$.
- Objective: learn a mapping $f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) \approx y$ by minimizing the empirical risk.
- Sub-tasks: classification (discrete $y$) and regression (continuous $y$).
- Engineering example: predicting the compressive strength of concrete from its mix proportions (regression).

**2. Unsupervised Learning** *(2 marks)*
- Data requirement: only inputs $\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^{N}$; no labels.
- Objective: discover hidden structure — clusters, low-dimensional manifolds, or association rules.
- Engineering example: grouping customers of a power utility into load-profile clusters using K-Means.

**3. Reinforcement Learning** *(2 marks)*
- Data requirement: interaction tuples $(s_t, a_t, r_{t+1}, s_{t+1})$ collected by an agent acting in an environment.
- Objective: learn a policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ that maximizes the expected discounted return $\mathbb{E}[G_t]$.
- Engineering example: training a bipedal robot to walk on uneven terrain.

**4. Semi-Supervised Learning** *(1 mark)*
- Data requirement: a small labeled set + a large unlabeled set.
- Objective: leverage unlabeled structure to improve a model that would otherwise be data-starved.
- Engineering example: classifying satellite imagery where manual labeling is expensive.

---

#### Model Solution — Part A(b) [7 Marks]

**Given:** $TP = 80$, $FP = 20$, $FN = 30$, $TN = 870$. Total $N = 1000$.

**Step 1 — Accuracy** *(1.5 marks)*

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} = \frac{80 + 870}{1000} = \frac{950}{1000} = 0.95$$

**Step 2 — Precision** *(1.5 marks)*

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{80}{80 + 20} = \frac{80}{100} = 0.80$$

**Step 3 — Recall** *(1.5 marks)*

$$\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{80}{80 + 30} = \frac{80}{110} \approx 0.727$$

**Step 4 — F1-Score** *(1.5 marks)*

$$F_1 = \frac{2 \times \text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} = \frac{2 \times 0.80 \times 0.727}{0.80 + 0.727} = \frac{1.1632}{1.527} \approx 0.762$$

**Step 5 — Comment** *(1 mark)*
Although accuracy is 95% (which looks impressive), the **class imbalance** is striking: positives are only $110/1000 = 11\%$ of the data. A trivial model that *always predicts negative* would also achieve ~89% accuracy, yet be useless. The low recall (72.7%) means the model is missing roughly 1 in 4 actual positive cases — a serious concern in high-stakes domains like medical diagnosis or fault detection. Hence, **accuracy alone is not a reliable metric** for imbalanced datasets; F1-score, precision, and recall must be reported jointly.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam – June 2024]**

**(a) [7 Marks]** With the aid of a neat block diagram, describe the standard end-to-end Machine Learning pipeline. Explain the importance of the train/validation/test split.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Derive the gradient descent update rule for a linear regression model with Mean Squared Error loss. State two conditions under which the algorithm is said to have converged.

---

#### Model Solution — Part B(a) [7 Marks]

**Pipeline (Block Diagram)** *(3 marks)*

The standard pipeline proceeds through the following stages (refer to the diagram in Section 4.2):

1. **Problem Definition** — frame the task (classification / regression / clustering) and choose a performance metric $P$.
2. **Data Collection** — gather raw samples from sensors, databases, or web sources.
3. **Data Preprocessing** — handle missing values (imputation / deletion), remove duplicates, and detect outliers.
4. **Feature Engineering** — encode categorical variables (one-hot, ordinal), scale numerical features (standardization / min-max), and perform feature selection.
5. **Data Splitting** — partition the data into **Training Set** (e.g., 70%), **Validation Set** (e.g., 15%), and **Test Set** (e.g., 15%).
6. **Model Training** — fit parameters $\theta$ by minimizing the loss on the training set.
7. **Hyperparameter Tuning** — use the validation set to choose learning rate $\eta$, regularization strength, tree depth, etc.
8. **Evaluation** — measure final performance on the **untouched** test set.
9. **Deployment & Monitoring** — serve the model and watch for data drift.

**Importance of Train/Validation/Test Split** *(4 marks)*

- The **training set** is used to learn the model parameters $\theta$.
- The **validation set** is used to tune hyperparameters and perform model selection — it provides an *unbiased* estimate of performance during development.
- The **test set** is used **only once**, at the very end, to estimate the model's **generalization error** on truly unseen data.
- **Why three sets, not two?** If we use the test set for hyperparameter tuning, the model indirectly *sees* the test data and we lose an honest measure of generalization. The validation set acts as a "sacrificial" proxy for the test set during development.
- A **typical split ratio** is $60\% / 20\% / 20\%$ or $70\% / 15\% / 15\%$. For very large datasets (millions of samples), the test split can be as small as 5%.

---

#### Model Solution — Part B(b) [7 Marks]

**Step 1 — Define the model and loss** *(1.5 marks)*

For a single training example $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$, the linear regression model is:

$$\hat{y}_i = f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i) = \theta^\top \mathbf{x}_i$$

The Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss over $N$ samples is:

$$\hat{R}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \big(y_i - \theta^\top \mathbf{x}_i\big)^2$$

**Step 2 — Compute the gradient** *(2 marks)*

Differentiating $\hat{R}(\theta)$ with respect to $\theta$:

$$\nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \theta^\top \mathbf{x}_i)^2 \right]$$

Apply the chain rule term-by-term:

$$\nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} 2 \cdot (y_i - \theta^\top \mathbf{x}_i) \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}(y_i - \theta^\top \mathbf{x}_i)$$

Since $\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}(y_i - \theta^\top \mathbf{x}_i) = -\mathbf{x}_i$:

$$\nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta) = -\frac{2}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \theta^\top \mathbf{x}_i) \, \mathbf{x}_i$$

**Step 3 — Gradient descent update rule** *(2 marks)*

The parameters are updated by moving in the direction opposite to the gradient, scaled by the learning rate $\eta$:

$$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \hat{R}\big(\theta^{(t)}\big)$$

Substituting the gradient:

$$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} + \frac{2\eta}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \big(y_i - {\theta^{(t)}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i\big) \, \mathbf{x}_i$$

**Step 4 — Convergence conditions** *(1.5 marks)*

The algorithm is said to have converged when **either** of the following holds:

1. **Gradient norm is small:** $\vert \vert \nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta^{(t)}) \vert \vert_2 < \epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is a small tolerance (e.g., $10^{-6}$). This means the loss surface is essentially flat — further updates change $\theta$ negligibly.
2. **Loss plateau:** $\vert \hat{R}(\theta^{(t+1)}) - \hat{R}(\theta^{(t)}) \vert < \epsilon$, i.e., the loss has stopped improving meaningfully.
3. **Maximum iterations reached:** $t \geq T_{\max}$ (a safety bound to prevent infinite loops).
4. **Early stopping on validation loss:** training halts when the validation loss fails to improve for $k$ consecutive epochs (e.g., $k = 10$).

*(Any two of the above for full marks.)*

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls (Read Before Writing Your Exam):**
> 1. **Confusing "features" and "labels":** In supervised learning, $\mathbf{x}$ = features (input), $y$ = label (output). Reversing them is an instant 1-mark deduction.
> 2. **Reporting only accuracy:** For imbalanced datasets, accuracy is misleading. Always compute **Precision, Recall, and F1-score** when the class distribution is skewed.
> 3. **Forgetting the validation set:** Many students split into *only* train and test, then tune hyperparameters on the test set. This is **data leakage** and will cost 2–3 marks.
> 4. **Mixing up clustering algorithms:** K-Means requires specifying $k$ in advance; DBSCAN does not. Examiners love this trap.
> 5. **Using `\|` inside a markdown table:** When writing equations in tabular form, vertical bars are interpreted as column separators. Use `\vert` or place the equation outside the table.
> 6. **Skipping the diagram in pipeline questions:** A 7-mark pipeline question **without** a block diagram typically caps at 5 marks. Always include one.
> 7. **Not stating the learning paradigm explicitly:** When asked to "explain an algorithm," always open with "This is a *supervised* learning algorithm because..." — examiners award marks for the framing.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

- **ML Definition (Mitchell):** A program learns from experience $\mathbf{E}$ to improve performance $\mathbf{P}$ on task $\mathbf{T}$.
- **Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM):** The cornerstone principle — minimize average loss on the training set.
- **Four Paradigms:** Supervised (labeled), Unsupervised (unlabeled), Reinforcement (reward), Semi-Supervised (mixed).
- **Supervised sub-tasks:** Classification (discrete $y$) vs Regression (continuous $y$).
- **Unsupervised sub-tasks:** Clustering, Dimensionality Reduction, Association Rule Mining.
- **Key metrics for classification:** Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score (always report together for imbalanced data).
- **Key metrics for regression:** MSE, RMSE, MAE.
- **RL objective:** Maximize $G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}$.
- **Gradient Descent update:** $\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta \nabla_\theta \hat{R}(\theta^{(t)})$.
- **Pipeline order:** Data → Preprocess → Features → Split → Train → Validate → Test → Deploy.
- **Split ratio:** 70/15/15 (train/val/test) is the KTU-recommended default.
- **Generalization > Memorization:** A model's true value is its performance on **unseen** data.
- **Overfitting:** Model too complex → high variance → fails on new data.
- **Underfitting:** Model too simple → high bias → fails on training data too.
- **Bias-Variance Tradeoff:** Total Error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Noise.
- **No Free Lunch Theorem:** No single algorithm is universally best — choice depends on data and task.
- **KTU Viva Favorites:** "Why is F1 preferred over accuracy in imbalanced problems?" / "What's the role of $\gamma$ in RL?" / "Why do we need a separate validation set?"
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** GNEST305 - INTRODUCTION TO ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DATA SCIENCE
> - **Module:** Module 1
> - **Topic:** Regression Models

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Regression** is a **supervised machine learning** technique used to model and analyze the relationship between a **dependent variable (target/output, $Y$)** and one or more **independent variables (predictors/features, $X$)**. The primary objective is to estimate a continuous, real-valued output by fitting a mathematical function to observed data.

In the KTU 2024 NEP-aligned framework for **GNEST305**, regression is positioned as the foundational **predictive modeling** paradigm under the broader umbrella of **Statistical Learning Theory**. It is formally expressed as:

$$\hat{Y} = f(X) + \epsilon$$

where:
- $\hat{Y}$ is the **predicted (estimated) value** of the dependent variable.
- $f(X)$ is the **regression function** mapping inputs to outputs.
- $\epsilon$ is the **irreducible error term** (random noise) assumed to be independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) with mean $\mu_{\epsilon} = 0$.

The learned function $f(X)$ is parameterized by a vector of weights $\boldsymbol{\theta} = \{\theta_0, \theta_1, \dots, \theta_n\}$ that are optimized to minimize a **loss function** (typically Mean Squared Error).

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Real Estate Advisor" Intuition

Imagine you are a **real estate advisor** in Kerala trying to estimate the **fair price of a house**. You don't guess randomly — instead, you look at historical data:

| Feature ($X$) | Observation |
|---|---|
| Area (sq. ft.) | Bigger houses cost more |
| Bedrooms | More bedrooms → higher price |
| Locality | Urban > Rural (generally) |
| Distance from city | Farther → cheaper |

You mentally build a **rule of thumb**:
> *"Price ≈ 2500 × Area + 50000 × Bedrooms − 10000 × Distance + BasePrice"*

This **rule of thumb** is exactly what a regression model learns! The **coefficients** (2500, 50000, −10000) are the **model parameters** ($\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3$) that the algorithm discovers by minimizing the difference between predicted and actual historical prices.

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Highlight:** Regression is a *parametric* approach (assumes a functional form) and is the gateway to understanding **Neural Networks** (where $f(X)$ becomes a non-linear composition of layers).

## 1.3 Taxonomy of Regression Models

The following hierarchy is the standard classification expected in KTU examinations:

| Type | Functional Form | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple Linear Regression** | $\hat{Y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 X$ | One predictor, linear trend |
| **Multiple Linear Regression** | $\hat{Y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 X_1 + \dots + \theta_n X_n$ | Multiple predictors, linear |
| **Polynomial Regression** | $\hat{Y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 X + \theta_2 X^2 + \dots$ | Non-linear curvature |
| **Ridge Regression (L2)** | Linear + $\lambda \sum \theta_i^2$ | Multicollinearity control |
| **Lasso Regression (L1)** | Linear + $\lambda \sum \vert \theta_i \vert$ | Feature selection |
| **Logistic Regression** | $\hat{Y} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\theta_0 + \theta_1 X)}}$ | Classification (despite name) |
| **Support Vector Regression** | $\epsilon$-insensitive loss | Robust to outliers |
| **Decision Tree Regression** | Piecewise constant splits | Non-parametric |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Statistical Learning Framework

The journey of regression under KTU's outcome-based education (OBE) begins with the **statistical model**:

$$Y = f(X) + \epsilon$$

The systematic decomposition is:
- **Systematic part** $f(X)$ — the predictable structure we wish to learn.
- **Stochastic part** $\epsilon$ — random noise, $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ for the standard OLS assumption.

### Why we cannot solve $f(X)$ exactly

In reality, $f(X)$ is an **unknown deterministic function** mapping inputs to outputs. We only observe a finite dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{m}$. The **goal of regression is to estimate** an approximation $\hat{f}(X)$ such that the expected prediction error on unseen data is minimized.

## 2.2 Simple Linear Regression — Detailed Mechanics

For a single feature $X$, the hypothesized model is:

$$\hat{y}^{(i)} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)}$$

- $\theta_0$ = **intercept** (the predicted $Y$ when $X = 0$).
- $\theta_1$ = **slope** (the average change in $Y$ for a unit change in $X$).

### 2.2.1 The Cost Function (Mean Squared Error)

The **Mean Squared Error (MSE)** is the canonical loss for regression:

$$J(\theta_0, \theta_1) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2 = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2$$

> [!NOTE]
> The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ is a mathematical convenience — it cancels out the exponent **2** during differentiation, making gradient formulas cleaner. **It does not change the optimal parameters.**

### 2.2.2 Two Methods to Find Optimal Parameters

| Method | Type | Formula | Pros / Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Normal Equation** | Closed-form (analytical) | $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y$ | Exact, but $O(n^3)$ — slow for large $n$ |
| **Gradient Descent** | Iterative (numerical) | $\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j}$ | Scalable, requires learning rate tuning |

## 2.3 Multiple Linear Regression (MLR)

For $n$ features, the model generalizes to:

$$\hat{y}^{(i)} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1^{(i)} + \theta_2 x_2^{(i)} + \dots + \theta_n x_n^{(i)}$$

In **vectorized matrix form**:

$$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\theta}$$

where:
- $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times (n+1)}$ is the **design matrix** (with a leading column of **1s** for $\theta_0$).
- $\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n+1) \times 1}$ is the parameter vector.
- $\hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 1}$ is the prediction vector.

The **MSE** in matrix form:

$$J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y})^T (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y})$$

## 2.4 Gradient Descent — The Iterative Workhorse

The **update rule** for each parameter $\theta_j$ is:

$$\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \frac{\partial J(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_j} = \theta_j - \frac{\alpha}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)}$$

where $\alpha$ is the **learning rate** (hyperparameter).

| Learning Rate | Effect |
|---|---|
| $\alpha$ **too small** | Slow convergence (takes many iterations) |
| $\alpha$ **too large** | Divergence / oscillation around minimum |
| $\alpha$ **just right** | Smooth, monotonic decrease in $J(\theta)$ |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Examiner's Note:** Students must remember that gradient descent **requires feature scaling** (standardization or min-max normalization) for fast convergence. Otherwise, elongated contour lines cause zig-zag paths.

## 2.5 The Normal Equation (Closed-Form Solution)

Setting the gradient $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{0}$ yields:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}} = \frac{1}{m} \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{0}$$

Solving:

$$\boxed{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*} = \left( \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}}$$

This is the **Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse solution** when $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$ is non-invertible (singular).

## 2.6 Polynomial Regression

A non-linear relationship is captured by introducing polynomial terms:

$$\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x + \theta_2 x^2 + \theta_3 x^3$$

This is still a **linear model** in parameters — the linearity refers to $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, not $X$. We can map it to MLR by setting $x_1 = x$, $x_2 = x^2$, $x_3 = x^3$.

## 2.7 Regularized Regression (Handling Overfitting)

### 2.7.1 Ridge Regression (L2 Penalty)

$$J_{\text{Ridge}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{n} \theta_j^2 \right]$$

- $\lambda$ is the **regularization strength** (hyperparameter).
- Shrinks coefficients toward zero but **never exactly zero**.

### 2.7.2 Lasso Regression (L1 Penalty)

$$J_{\text{Lasso}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{n} \vert \theta_j \vert \right]$$

- Produces **sparse models** (drives some $\theta_j$ to exactly **0**).
- Useful for **automatic feature selection**.

### 2.7.3 Elastic Net (L1 + L2 Combined)

$$J_{\text{EN}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2 + \lambda \left( \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{n} \vert \theta_j \vert + (1 - \alpha) \sum_{j=1}^{n} \theta_j^2 \right) \right]$$

## 2.8 KTU High-Yield Formula Cheat Sheet

| # | Formula | Symbol Meaning | KTU Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x$ | Simple linear hypothesis | Model definition |
| 2 | $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}$ | Vectorized hypothesis | MLR model |
| 3 | $J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum (\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)})^2$ | MSE cost | Optimization objective |
| 4 | $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$ | Normal equation | Closed-form solution |
| 5 | $\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j}$ | GD update | Iterative learning |
| 6 | $R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{\text{res}}}{SS_{\text{tot}}}$ | Coefficient of determination | Model evaluation |
| 7 | $R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1-R^2)\frac{m-1}{m-n-1}$ | Adjusted R² | MLR with many features |
| 8 | $J_{\text{Ridge}} = \text{MSE} + \lambda \sum \theta_j^2$ | L2 penalty | Ridge |
| 9 | $J_{\text{Lasso}} = \text{MSE} + \lambda \sum \vert \theta_j \vert$ | L1 penalty | Lasso |
| 10 | $\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\sum (\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)})^2}$ | Root MSE | Interpretable metric |
| 11 | $\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{m} \sum \vert \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \vert$ | Mean Absolute Error | Robust to outliers |
| 12 | $\text{MAPE} = \frac{100\%}{m} \sum \left\vert \frac{\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)}}{y^{(i)}} \right\vert$ | Mean Abs. % Error | Scale-independent metric |

## 2.9 Model Evaluation Metrics — Deeper View

The **R² (coefficient of determination)** measures the proportion of variance explained:

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{\text{residual}}}{SS_{\text{total}}} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} (y^{(i)} - \hat{y}^{(i)})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} (y^{(i)} - \bar{y})^2}$$

- $R^2 = 1$ → perfect fit.
- $R^2 = 0$ → model is as good as predicting the mean.
- $R^2 < 0$ → model is worse than the mean (catastrophic underfitting).

> [!NOTE]
> In MLR, $R^2$ **always increases** (or stays the same) as we add features — even useless ones! Hence we use the **Adjusted R²** which penalizes unnecessary features.

## 2.10 The Bias-Variance Tradeoff

| Concept | High Bias | High Variance |
|---|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Underfitting | Overfitting |
| **Training error** | High | Low |
| **Test error** | High | High |
| **Model complexity** | Too simple (e.g., linear for non-linear data) | Too complex (e.g., degree-10 polynomial for 5 points) |
| **Remedy** | Add features, use polynomial, reduce regularization | More data, feature selection, increase $\lambda$ |

## 2.11 Real-World Engineering Applications

| Domain | Application |
|---|---|
| **Civil Engineering** | Predicting concrete strength from mix proportions |
| **Electrical** | Forecasting power consumption from temperature/humidity |
| **Mechanical** | Estimating tool wear from operating parameters |
| **Economics** | Demand forecasting for commodities |
| **Healthcare** | Predicting patient recovery time from vitals |
| **IoT/AIoT** | Smart sensor calibration & predictive maintenance |

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation I: Normal Equation for Simple Linear Regression

**Given** $m$ data points $\{(x^{(1)}, y^{(1)}), (x^{(2)}, y^{(2)}), \dots, (x^{(m)}, y^{(m)})\}$, we want to find $\theta_0, \theta_1$ that minimize:

$$J(\theta_0, \theta_1) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2$$

**Step 1:** Take the partial derivative of $J$ w.r.t. $\theta_0$.

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_0} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)$$

**Step 2:** Take the partial derivative of $J$ w.r.t. $\theta_1$.

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) x^{(i)}$$

**Step 3:** Set both partial derivatives to **zero** (first-order optimality condition).

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_0} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) = 0$$

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) x^{(i)} = 0$$

**Step 4:** Expand the first equation.

$$m \theta_0 + \theta_1 \sum_{i=1}^{m} x^{(i)} - \sum_{i=1}^{m} y^{(i)} = 0$$

$$\theta_0 = \bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x}$$

where $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{m}\sum x^{(i)}$ and $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{m}\sum y^{(i)}$.

**Step 5:** Expand the second equation and substitute $\theta_0$ from Step 4.

$$\sum_{i=1}^{m} \theta_0 x^{(i)} + \theta_1 \sum_{i=1}^{m} (x^{(i)})^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{m} x^{(i)} y^{(i)} = 0$$

Substituting $\theta_0 = \bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x}$:

$$(\bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x}) \sum_{i=1}^{m} x^{(i)} + \theta_1 \sum_{i=1}^{m} (x^{(i)})^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{m} x^{(i)} y^{(i)} = 0$$

Using $\sum x^{(i)} = m \bar{x}$:

$$m \bar{x} \bar{y} - \theta_1 m (\bar{x})^2 + \theta_1 \sum (x^{(i)})^2 - \sum x^{(i)} y^{(i)} = 0$$

**Step 6:** Solve for $\theta_1$.

$$\theta_1 \left[ \sum (x^{(i)})^2 - m (\bar{x})^2 \right] = \sum x^{(i)} y^{(i)} - m \bar{x} \bar{y}$$

Recognize the bracketed term as $m \cdot \text{Var}(X)$ and the right-hand side as $m \cdot \text{Cov}(X, Y)$:

$$\boxed{\theta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} (x^{(i)} - \bar{x})(y^{(i)} - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} (x^{(i)} - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\text{Var}(X)}}$$

$$\boxed{\theta_0 = \bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x}}$$

> [!NOTE]
> This is the **classic OLS estimator**. KTU examiners frequently ask students to derive this in Part B (14-mark) questions.

## 3.2 Derivation II: Matrix-Form Normal Equation for MLR

**Given** the MSE in matrix form:

$$J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y})^T (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y})$$

**Step 1:** Expand the quadratic.

$$J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ \boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\theta} - 2 \boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y} \right]$$

**Step 2:** Take the gradient w.r.t. $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

Using the matrix calculus identities:
- $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{A}^T$
- $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol{\theta}) = 2 \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol{\theta}$ (when $\mathbf{A}$ is symmetric)

$$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ 2 \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\theta} - 2 \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} \right]$$

$$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{m} \left[ \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} \right]$$

**Step 3:** Set gradient to zero.

$$\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}$$

**Step 4:** Solve for $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ by left-multiplying with $(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}$.

$$\boxed{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*} = \left( \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The matrix $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n+1) \times (n+1)}$ must be **invertible** (i.e., $\det(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) \neq 0$). This fails when:
> - Features are **linearly dependent** (perfect multicollinearity).
> - $m < n$ (more features than samples).
>
> **Solution:** Use **pseudoinverse** $\mathbf{X}^{+} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T$ via SVD, or apply **regularization** to make $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I}$ invertible.

## 3.3 Derivation III: Gradient Descent Update Rule for Linear Regression

**Goal:** Find the negative gradient direction for each $\theta_j$.

Starting from the MSE:

$$J(\theta_0, \theta_1) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2$$

**Step 1:** Compute the partial derivative of $J$ w.r.t. $\theta_j$ (for $j \geq 1$).

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}^{(i)}}{\partial \theta_j}$$

**Step 2:** Since $\hat{y}^{(i)} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1^{(i)} + \dots + \theta_n x_n^{(i)}$, we have $\frac{\partial \hat{y}^{(i)}}{\partial \theta_j} = x_j^{(i)}$.

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)}$$

**Step 3:** Apply the gradient descent update:

$$\boxed{\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)}}$$

For $\theta_0$ (intercept), $x_0^{(i)} = 1$ always, so the same formula applies.

### Vectorized Form of Gradient Descent

$$\boldsymbol{\theta} := \boldsymbol{\theta} - \frac{\alpha}{m} \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y})$$

## 3.4 Derivation IV: Ridge Regression Closed-Form

The Ridge cost function is:

$$J_{\text{Ridge}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y})^T (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y}) + \lambda \boldsymbol{\theta}^T \boldsymbol{\theta} \right]$$

**Step 1:** Take the gradient and set to zero.

$$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J_{\text{Ridge}} = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ 2\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\theta} - 2\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} + 2\lambda \boldsymbol{\theta} \right] = \mathbf{0}$$

**Step 2:** Rearrange.

$$(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I}) \boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$$

**Step 3:** Solve.

$$\boxed{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{Ridge}}^{*} = \left( \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}}$$

> [!NOTE]
> The $\lambda \mathbf{I}$ term **guarantees invertibility** even when $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$ is singular. This is why Ridge regression is the standard fix for multicollinearity.

## 3.5 Worked Numerical Example (KTU-Style)

**Problem:** Given data points $(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 4)$, fit a simple linear regression $\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x$ using the Normal Equation.

**Step 1:** Compute the means.

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1+2+3+4}{4} = 2.5, \quad \bar{y} = \frac{2+3+5+4}{4} = 3.5$$

**Step 2:** Compute numerator (covariance sum) and denominator (variance sum).

| $x^{(i)}$ | $y^{(i)}$ | $x^{(i)} - \bar{x}$ | $y^{(i)} - \bar{y}$ | Product | $(x^{(i)} - \bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | −1.5 | −1.5 | 2.25 | 2.25 |
| 2 | 3 | −0.5 | −0.5 | 0.25 | 0.25 |
| 3 | 5 |  0.5 |  1.5 | 0.75 | 0.25 |
| 4 | 4 |  1.5 |  0.5 | 0.75 | 2.25 |
| **Sum** | | | | **4.00** | **5.00** |

**Step 3:** Compute $\theta_1$.

$$\theta_1 = \frac{\sum (x^{(i)} - \bar{x})(y^{(i)} - \bar{y})}{\sum (x^{(i)} - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{4.00}{5.00} = 0.8$$

**Step 4:** Compute $\theta_0$.

$$\theta_0 = \bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x} = 3.5 - 0.8 \times 2.5 = 3.5 - 2.0 = 1.5$$

**Step 5:** Final fitted model.

$$\hat{y} = 1.5 + 0.8 x$$

**Step 6:** Compute $R^2$ to verify fit quality.

Predictions: $\hat{y}(1) = 2.3$, $\hat{y}(2) = 3.1$, $\hat{y}(3) = 3.9$, $\hat{y}(4) = 4.7$.

$$SS_{\text{res}} = (2-2.3)^2 + (3-3.1)^2 + (5-3.9)^2 + (4-4.7)^2 = 0.09 + 0.01 + 1.21 + 0.49 = 1.80$$

$$SS_{\text{tot}} = (2-3.5)^2 + (3-3.5)^2 + (5-3.5)^2 + (4-3.5)^2 = 2.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 = 5.00$$

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{1.80}{5.00} = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64$$

The model explains **64%** of the variance — a moderate fit.

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Question 1** `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**Define regression. Differentiate between simple linear regression and multiple linear regression.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Regression** is a supervised learning technique used to predict a continuous dependent variable $Y$ from one or more independent variables $X$ by learning a mapping function $f: X \to Y$.

| Feature | Simple Linear Regression | Multiple Linear Regression |
|---|---|---|
| Number of predictors | **One** | **Two or more** |
| Functional form | $\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x$ | $\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \theta_2 x_2 + \dots$ |
| Visualization | 2D straight line | n-dimensional hyperplane |
| Complexity | Low | Higher; risk of multicollinearity |

**(1 mark for definition, 2 marks for clear differentiation with formulas.)**

---

### **Question 2** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**What is the cost function in linear regression? Why is Mean Squared Error (MSE) preferred over Mean Absolute Error (MAE)?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

The **cost function** quantifies the error between predicted values $\hat{y}^{(i)}$ and actual values $y^{(i)}$. For linear regression, the standard cost is the **Mean Squared Error**:

$$J(\theta_0, \theta_1) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2$$

**Why MSE is preferred:**
1. **Differentiable** everywhere — gradient descent optimization works smoothly. (MAE is not differentiable at zero error.)
2. **Quadratic penalty** — larger errors are penalized more heavily, driving the model to fit outliers more aggressively.
3. **Closed-form solution exists** — Normal Equation $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$ is derivable.

**(1 mark for cost function formula, 2 marks for the three reasons.)**

---

## PART B — 14-Mark Questions (ESE Module Internal Choice)

### **Question A** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**(a)** Derive the normal equation for simple linear regression. Show all steps clearly. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Given the following data, fit a linear regression model using the normal equation and predict $y$ when $x = 6$.

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 2 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 6 |

Compute $R^2$ for the fit. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Part (a) — Derivation (7 marks):**

The simple linear model: $\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x$.

The MSE cost function:

$$J(\theta_0, \theta_1) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right)^2$$

Setting partial derivatives to zero:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_0} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) = 0 \quad (1)$$

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \theta_0 + \theta_1 x^{(i)} - y^{(i)} \right) x^{(i)} = 0 \quad (2)$$

From (1): $m\theta_0 + \theta_1 \sum x^{(i)} = \sum y^{(i)} \Rightarrow \theta_0 = \bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x}$.

Substituting into (2) and solving:

$$\theta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} (x^{(i)} - \bar{x})(y^{(i)} - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} (x^{(i)} - \bar{x})^2}$$

$$\theta_0 = \bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x}$$

**Part (b) — Numerical Computation (7 marks):**

Compute means: $\bar{x} = \frac{1+2+3+4+5}{5} = 3$, $\bar{y} = \frac{2+4+5+4+6}{5} = 4.2$.

| $x^{(i)}$ | $y^{(i)}$ | $x^{(i)} - 3$ | $y^{(i)} - 4.2$ | Product | $(x^{(i)} - 3)^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | −2 | −2.2 | 4.4 | 4 |
| 2 | 4 | −1 | −0.2 | 0.2 | 1 |
| 3 | 5 |  0 |  0.8 | 0.0 | 0 |
| 4 | 4 |  1 | −0.2 | −0.2 | 1 |
| 5 | 6 |  2 |  1.8 | 3.6 | 4 |
| **Sum** | | | | **8.0** | **10** |

$$\theta_1 = \frac{8.0}{10} = 0.8$$

$$\theta_0 = 4.2 - 0.8 \times 3 = 4.2 - 2.4 = 1.8$$

**Fitted model:** $\hat{y} = 1.8 + 0.8 x$.

**Prediction at $x = 6$:** $\hat{y} = 1.8 + 0.8 \times 6 = 1.8 + 4.8 = \mathbf{6.6}$.

**Compute $R^2$:**

Predictions: $\hat{y}(1) = 2.6$, $\hat{y}(2) = 3.4$, $\hat{y}(3) = 4.2$, $\hat{y}(4) = 5.0$, $\hat{y}(5) = 5.8$.

$$SS_{\text{res}} = (2-2.6)^2 + (4-3.4)^2 + (5-4.2)^2 + (4-5.0)^2 + (6-5.8)^2$$
$$= 0.36 + 0.36 + 0.64 + 1.00 + 0.04 = 2.40$$

$$SS_{\text{tot}} = (2-4.2)^2 + (4-4.2)^2 + (5-4.2)^2 + (4-4.2)^2 + (6-4.2)^2$$
$$= 4.84 + 0.04 + 0.64 + 0.04 + 3.24 = 8.80$$

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{2.40}{8.80} = 1 - 0.2727 = \mathbf{0.7273}$$

The model explains **72.73%** of variance — a good fit.

---

### **Question B** `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**(a)** Explain the gradient descent algorithm for linear regression. List and explain three variants of gradient descent. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** What is regularization? Compare Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) regression with suitable mathematical formulations. When would you prefer one over the other? **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Part (a) — Gradient Descent for Linear Regression (7 marks):**

Gradient descent is an **iterative optimization algorithm** that minimizes $J(\theta_0, \theta_1, \dots, \theta_n)$ by updating parameters in the direction of steepest descent (negative gradient).

**Algorithm steps:**
1. Initialize $\theta_j$ (often to 0 or small random values).
2. Compute predictions: $\hat{y}^{(i)} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1^{(i)} + \dots + \theta_n x_n^{(i)}$.
3. Compute the gradient: $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} (\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)}) x_j^{(i)}$.
4. Update simultaneously:
   $$\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j}$$
5. Repeat until convergence ($\vert J^{(t)} - J^{(t-1)} \vert < \epsilon$) or max iterations.

**Three variants of gradient descent:**

| Variant | Data per Update | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Batch GD** | Uses **all $m$ samples** per iteration | Stable convergence, deterministic | Slow for large $m$; needs full dataset in memory |
| **Stochastic GD (SGD)** | Uses **one sample** per iteration | Fast, can escape local minima, online learning | Noisy convergence path |
| **Mini-batch GD** | Uses **batch of $b$ samples** ($1 < b < m$) per iteration | Balance between speed and stability; GPU-friendly | Requires tuning batch size $b$ |

**Part (b) — Regularization: Ridge vs Lasso (7 marks):**

**Regularization** is a technique to **prevent overfitting** by adding a penalty term to the cost function that discourages large parameter values.

**Ridge Regression (L2):**

$$J_{\text{Ridge}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{m} (\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)})^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{n} \theta_j^2 \right]$$

Closed-form solution: $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{Ridge}} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$.

- Shrinks coefficients **toward zero** but never exactly zero.
- Handles **multicollinearity** effectively.
- All features retained.

**Lasso Regression (L1):**

$$J_{\text{Lasso}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{m} (\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)})^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{n} \vert \theta_j \vert \right]$$

- Drives some coefficients to **exactly zero** → automatic **feature selection**.
- Produces **sparse, interpretable models**.
- Not closed-form; solved via **coordinate descent** or **LARS**.

**When to prefer which:**

| Scenario | Preferred Method |
|---|---|
| Multicollinearity, all features important | **Ridge** |
| High-dimensional data, need feature selection | **Lasso** |
| Many correlated features, want both effects | **Elastic Net** |
| $m \ll n$ (fewer samples than features) | **Lasso** (sparsity helps) |

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:**
> 1. **Gradient Descent Convergence:** Many students forget to mention the **simultaneous update** of parameters — sequential updates can yield incorrect results. **(Lose 1 mark)**
> 2. **MSE vs MAE:** Confusing the two cost functions is a common mistake — MSE squares, MAE uses absolute value. **(Lose 1 mark)**
> 3. **R² Interpretation:** Students often forget that R² can be **negative** (model worse than mean). **(Lose 0.5 mark)**
> 4. **Ridge vs Lasso:** Writing the penalty as $\lambda \sum \theta_i^2$ for Lasso is a **fatal error** — Lasso uses **absolute values**, not squares. **(Lose 2 marks)**
> 5. **Multicollinearity:** OLS fails when features are correlated — Ridge fixes this; students often skip this distinction. **(Lose 1 mark)**

---

## Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist for KTU 2024 ESE:**

- **Regression** predicts **continuous** outputs; **Classification** predicts **discrete labels**.
- **Simple Linear Regression** has one feature; **Multiple Linear Regression** has $n \geq 2$ features.
- **Cost function** is **Mean Squared Error (MSE)**: $J = \frac{1}{2m}\sum(\hat{y} - y)^2$.
- **Normal Equation** is the **closed-form OLS solution**: $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$.
- **Gradient Descent** is **iterative**, requires tuning of learning rate $\alpha$ and feature scaling.
- **Three GD variants:** Batch (stable/slow), Stochastic (fast/noisy), Mini-batch (balanced).
- **R²** measures variance explained: $R^2 = 1 - SS_{\text{res}}/SS_{\text{tot}}$.
- **Adjusted R²** penalizes extra features: $R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1-R^2)\frac{m-1}{m-n-1}$.
- **Ridge (L2)** shrinks coefficients; good for **multicollinearity**.
- **Lasso (L1)** produces **sparse models**; good for **feature selection**.
- **Polynomial Regression** models **non-linear** trends using $x, x^2, x^3, \dots$.
- **Bias-Variance Tradeoff:** Simple models = high bias, complex models = high variance.
- **OLS Assumptions:** Linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality, no multicollinearity.
- **Evaluation Metrics:** MAE, MSE, RMSE, R², Adjusted R².
- **Mean of X and Y** appears in intercept formula: $\theta_0 = \bar{y} - \theta_1 \bar{x}$.
- **Slope** = Covariance(X,Y) / Variance(X).

# Section 1 — Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Classification Model** is a supervised machine learning technique that learns a mapping function $f: X \rightarrow Y$ from a labeled training dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n}$, where $x^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is a feature vector with $m$ attributes and $y^{(i)} \in \{C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k\}$ is a discrete class label, in order to predict the categorical output for new, unseen instances.

In simpler terms, a **Classification Model** is a function that sorts incoming data into predefined buckets (classes) based on patterns it has already seen during training. The keyword here is **"discrete"** — we are not predicting a quantity (like height or price); we are predicting a *category* (Yes/No, Spam/Not-Spam, Disease/Healthy).

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU High-Yield Distinction**:
> - **Classification** → Output is a *categorical/discrete* label.
> - **Regression** → Output is a *continuous* real-valued number.
> This distinction is a guaranteed **Part-A question** in every KTU exam cycle.

## 1.2 Real-World Analogy — The Email Spam Filter

Imagine you are a postal worker who has spent years delivering mail. Over time, you have developed a strong "sixth sense" — you can glance at the sender, subject line, and keywords inside a letter and instantly decide whether to drop it in the **"Inbox"** tray or the **"Spam"** tray.

You did not memorize every rule. Instead, you learned a *pattern*:
- "FREE!!!" in the subject → probably spam.
- Email from your boss with a meeting agenda → probably not spam.

A **Classification Model** does exactly this. It studies a historical dataset (emails you already labeled as spam or not spam), extracts statistical patterns, and builds a mathematical rule to classify future, never-before-seen emails. The "postal worker" is the trained model; the "letters" are the test instances.

> [!TIP]
> **Other Real-World Examples of Classification:**
> - **Medical Diagnosis**: Predicting whether a tumor is *benign* or *malignant*.
> - **Credit Scoring**: Approving or rejecting a loan application.
> - **Image Recognition**: Tagging a photo as *cat, dog, or bird*.
> - **Sentiment Analysis**: Classifying a tweet as *positive, negative, or neutral*.

## 1.3 The Three Pillars of Any Classification Problem

Any classification task, no matter how complex, is defined by these **three** components. Memorize this — KTU examiners love testing this:

| Pillar | Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Feature Vector** | $x = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m)$ | The measurable input attributes | `[Outlook=Sunny, Temp=Hot, Humidity=High]` |
| **Class Label** | $y \in \{C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k\}$ | The discrete category to predict | `{Yes, No}` for "Play Tennis" |
| **Hypothesis Function** | $h_\theta(x)$ | The learned mapping $X \rightarrow Y$ | The trained Naive Bayes model |

## 1.4 The Working Example We Will Use Throughout

To keep things concrete, this module will walk through the **"Play Tennis"** decision problem — a benchmark dataset used in classical AI/ML textbooks. The question is: *"Given the weather conditions, should we play tennis today?"*

> [!NOTE]
> The dataset has **14 historical days** and **4 features** (Outlook, Temperature, Humidity, Wind). The class label is binary: **Yes** (play) or **No** (don't play). We will use the **Naive Bayes Classifier** to build the model because it has a transparent, hand-computable mathematical formulation — perfect for a KTU board exam.

This example will be the spine of Sections 2, 3, and 4.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# Section 2 — Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Naive Bayes Classifier — Theoretical Foundation

**Naive Bayes** is a *probabilistic* classifier grounded directly in **Bayes' Theorem** from probability theory. It is called "naive" because it makes a strong simplifying assumption: **all features are conditionally independent of each other given the class label**.

While this assumption is rarely true in the real world (e.g., humidity and outlook are correlated), it dramatically simplifies computation and still produces surprisingly accurate results — which is why Naive Bayes is a staple in spam filtering, sentiment analysis, and medical diagnosis.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight**: Naive Bayes falls under the "Probabilistic Learning" paradigm in the GNEST305 syllabus. The examiner expects you to (1) state Bayes' Theorem, (2) explain the "naive" independence assumption, and (3) solve a numerical problem end-to-end.

## 2.2 Derivation of the Decision Rule (Step-by-Step Logic)

The classifier must decide which class $C_k$ is most probable given the observed feature vector $x = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m)$. Mathematically, we want:

$$
\hat{y} = \arg\max_{C_k \in \{Yes, No\}} P(C_k \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m)
$$

We cannot compute this posterior directly, so we apply **Bayes' Theorem**:

$$
P(C_k \mid x) = \frac{P(x \mid C_k) \cdot P(C_k)}{P(x)}
$$

Since $P(x)$ is the same constant for every class (it does not depend on $C_k$), we can ignore it for comparison and write:

$$
\hat{y} = \arg\max_{C_k} P(C_k) \cdot P(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m \mid C_k)
$$

Now we apply the **chain rule of probability**:

$$
P(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m \mid C_k) = P(x_1 \mid C_k) \cdot P(x_2 \mid x_1, C_k) \cdot P(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2, C_k) \cdots
$$

This grows computationally infeasible. The **Naive Independence Assumption** states:

> Given the class $C_k$, every feature $x_i$ is independent of every other feature $x_j$.

This collapses the chain rule into a simple product of marginals:

$$
P(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m \mid C_k) \approx \prod_{j=1}^{m} P(x_j \mid C_k)
$$

**Final Decision Rule for Naive Bayes:**

$$
\boxed{\hat{y} = \arg\max_{C_k} \; P(C_k) \cdot \prod_{j=1}^{m} P(x_j \mid C_k)}
$$

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet (High-Yield Cheat Sheet)

> [!TIP]
> This table is your **exam-day survival kit**. Memorize the symbols, meanings, and units.

| # | Symbol / Formula | Name | Meaning | Used For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $P(C_k)$ | **Prior Probability** | How frequent class $C_k$ is in the training data | Starting belief before seeing evidence |
| 2 | $P(x_j \mid C_k)$ | **Likelihood** | Probability of feature $x_j$ occurring *given* class $C_k$ | Evidence from each attribute |
| 3 | $P(C_k \mid x)$ | **Posterior Probability** | Updated belief after seeing all features | Final decision quantity |
| 4 | $P(x)$ | **Evidence / Marginal** | Normalizing constant (same for all classes) | Can be ignored during $\arg\max$ |
| 5 | $P(C_k) \prod_{j=1}^{m} P(x_j \vert C_k)$ | **Naive Bayes Score** | Unnormalized posterior for class $C_k$ | Used to rank candidate classes |
| 6 | $\arg\max_{C_k}$ | **Argmax Operator** | Returns the class with the highest score | The actual predicted label $\hat{y}$ |
| 7 | $P(x_j = v \mid C_k) = \frac{\text{count}(x_j = v, C_k)}{\text{count}(C_k)}$ | **Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE)** | Frequency-based estimate of likelihood | Tabulating the training data |
| 8 | $\hat{P}(x_j = v \mid C_k) = \frac{\text{count}(x_j = v, C_k) + 1}{\text{count}(C_k) + \vert V_j \vert}$ | **Laplace Smoothing** | Avoids zero-probability for unseen values | When a feature value never co-occurs with a class |

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistake**: Students often write $P(x \mid C_k)$ as the **likelihood** but mistakenly call it the "posterior". Remember: **Likelihood = evidence given the class; Posterior = belief about the class given the evidence.** They are inverses (in direction), related through Bayes' Theorem.

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

Naive Bayes classifiers are deployed in:
- **Email gateways** (Gmail, Outlook spam filters).
- **Medical decision support systems** (calculating disease risk from symptoms).
- **Text classification pipelines** (news categorization, sentiment scoring).
- **Real-time recommendation engines** (low-latency probabilistic scoring).

Its main engineering virtues are: **lightning-fast training, low memory footprint, and graceful handling of high-dimensional sparse data** — which is why it is the "first model to try" in any new text-classification project.

# Section 3 — Step-by-Step Derivation & Worked Example

## 3.1 The "Play Tennis" Training Dataset (14 Days)

Below is the complete labeled dataset. **Memorize the structure** — KTU examiners may give a *slightly different* version and expect you to re-do the calculations.

| Day | Outlook | Temperature | Humidity | Wind | **Play (Class)** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | Sunny | Hot | High | Weak | **No** |
| 2 | Sunny | Hot | High | Strong | **No** |
| 3 | Overcast | Hot | High | Weak | **Yes** |
| 4 | Rain | Mild | High | Weak | **Yes** |
| 5 | Rain | Cool | Normal | Weak | **Yes** |
| 6 | Rain | Cool | Normal | Strong | **No** |
| 7 | Overcast | Cool | Normal | Strong | **Yes** |
| 8 | Sunny | Mild | High | Weak | **No** |
| 9 | Sunny | Cool | Normal | Weak | **Yes** |
| 10 | Rain | Mild | Normal | Weak | **Yes** |
| 11 | Sunny | Mild | Normal | Strong | **Yes** |
| 12 | Overcast | Mild | High | Strong | **Yes** |
| 13 | Overcast | Hot | Normal | Weak | **Yes** |
| 14 | Rain | Mild | High | Strong | **No** |

**Test Query (Day 15)**: `Outlook = Sunny`, `Temp = Cool`, `Humidity = High`, `Wind = Strong`. Should we play tennis?

## 3.2 Step 1 — Compute the Prior Probabilities $P(\text{Yes})$ and $P(\text{No})$

We count the number of days labeled "Yes" and "No" out of the total 14.

$$
P(\text{Yes}) = \frac{\text{Number of "Yes" days}}{\text{Total days}} = \frac{9}{14} \approx 0.6429
$$

$$
P(\text{No}) = \frac{\text{Number of "No" days}}{\text{Total days}} = \frac{5}{14} \approx 0.3571
$$

**Sanity check:** $P(\text{Yes}) + P(\text{No}) = \frac{9}{14} + \frac{5}{14} = \frac{14}{14} = 1.0$ ✓

> [!NOTE]
> The priors reflect the **base rate** of play in our training history. On most historical days, tennis was played, so the model starts with a slight bias toward "Yes" — but the evidence from the features can override this.

## 3.3 Step 2 — Build the Likelihood Tables (Frequency Tables)

We need $P(x_j \mid C_k)$ for every feature value and every class. The general formula is:

$$
P(x_j = v \mid C_k) = \frac{\text{count}(x_j = v \text{ AND } C_k)}{\text{count}(C_k)}
$$

### Table A — Outlook (3 values: Sunny, Overcast, Rain)

| Outlook | Yes (out of 9) | $P(\text{Outlook} \mid \text{Yes})$ | No (out of 5) | $P(\text{Outlook} \mid \text{No})$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Sunny | 2 | $2/9$ | 3 | $3/5$ |
| Overcast | 4 | $4/9$ | 0 | $0/5$ |
| Rain | 3 | $3/9$ | 2 | $2/5$ |
| **Total** | **9** | **1.0** | **5** | **1.0** |

### Table B — Temperature (3 values: Hot, Mild, Cool)

| Temperature | Yes (out of 9) | $P(\text{Temp} \mid \text{Yes})$ | No (out of 5) | $P(\text{Temp} \mid \text{No})$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Hot | 2 | $2/9$ | 2 | $2/5$ |
| Mild | 4 | $4/9$ | 2 | $2/5$ |
| Cool | 3 | $3/9$ | 1 | $1/5$ |

### Table C — Humidity (2 values: High, Normal)

| Humidity | Yes (out of 9) | $P(\text{Humidity} \mid \text{Yes})$ | No (out of 5) | $P(\text{Humidity} \mid \text{No})$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| High | 3 | $3/9$ | 4 | $4/5$ |
| Normal | 6 | $6/9$ | 1 | $1/5$ |

### Table D — Wind (2 values: Weak, Strong)

| Wind | Yes (out of 9) | $P(\text{Wind} \mid \text{Yes})$ | No (out of 5) | $P(\text{Wind} \mid \text{No})$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Weak | 6 | $6/9$ | 2 | $2/5$ |
| Strong | 3 | $3/9$ | 3 | $3/5$ |

> [!WARNING]
> **Zero-Probability Trap**: Notice that $P(\text{Overcast} \mid \text{No}) = 0/5 = 0$. If our test instance had `Outlook = Overcast`, the entire product for class "No" would collapse to zero. In real-world systems, this is fixed using **Laplace Smoothing** (add-1 to numerator, add-$\vert V \vert$ to denominator). In a KTU exam, you may be asked to apply Laplace smoothing if the test query hits a zero-count cell.

## 3.4 Step 3 — Apply the Naive Bayes Decision Rule

Our test instance is $x = (\text{Sunny}, \text{Cool}, \text{High}, \text{Strong})$. We need to compare:

$$
P(\text{Yes} \mid x) \;\propto\; P(\text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{Cool} \mid \text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{High} \mid \text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{Strong} \mid \text{Yes})
$$

$$
P(\text{No} \mid x) \;\propto\; P(\text{No}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{No}) \cdot P(\text{Cool} \mid \text{No}) \cdot P(\text{High} \mid \text{No}) \cdot P(\text{Strong} \mid \text{No})
$$

### Computation for Class = Yes

$$
P(\text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{Cool} \mid \text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{High} \mid \text{Yes}) \cdot P(\text{Strong} \mid \text{Yes})
$$

$$
= \frac{9}{14} \cdot \frac{2}{9} \cdot \frac{3}{9} \cdot \frac{3}{9} \cdot \frac{3}{9}
$$

$$
= \frac{9 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3}{14 \times 9 \times 9 \times 9 \times 9}
$$

$$
= \frac{486}{91854} \approx 0.00529
$$

### Computation for Class = No

$$
P(\text{No}) \cdot P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{No}) \cdot P(\text{Cool} \mid \text{No}) \cdot P(\text{High} \mid \text{No}) \cdot P(\text{Strong} \mid \text{No})
$$

$$
= \frac{5}{14} \cdot \frac{3}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{3}{5}
$$

$$
= \frac{5 \times 3 \times 1 \times 4 \times 3}{14 \times 5 \times 5 \times 5 \times 5}
$$

$$
= \frac{180}{8750} \approx 0.02057
$$

## 3.5 Step 4 — Normalize the Posteriors (Optional but Examiner-Friendly)

The two values 0.00529 and 0.02057 are unnormalized scores. To convert them into true probabilities that sum to 1, we divide by their sum:

$$
P(\text{Yes} \mid x) = \frac{0.00529}{0.00529 + 0.02057} = \frac{0.00529}{0.02586} \approx 0.2046
$$

$$
P(\text{No} \mid x) = \frac{0.02057}{0.00529 + 0.02057} = \frac{0.02057}{0.02586} \approx 0.7954
$$

## 3.6 Step 5 — Make the Final Prediction

$$
\boxed{\hat{y} = \arg\max_{C_k} \{ P(\text{Yes} \mid x), P(\text{No} \mid x) \} = \arg\max \{0.2046, \; 0.7954\} = \text{No}}
$$

**Conclusion**: The model predicts we should **NOT play tennis** on a Sunny, Cool, High-Humidity, Strong-Wind day. The model's confidence in "No" is **79.54%**.

> [!TIP]
> **Why did "No" win despite the prior favoring "Yes"?** Three features (Sunny, Cool, High) push strongly toward "No" — their likelihoods under "No" are all higher than under "Yes". The single feature (Strong wind) is equally likely under both classes, so it acts as a tie-breaker. This is a classic example of **evidence overcoming the prior** — a core Bayesian principle.

## 3.7 Analytical Matrix — Summary of the Decision

| Quantity | Class = Yes | Class = No | Winner |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Prior $P(C_k)$ | $9/14 = 0.6429$ | $5/14 = 0.3571$ | Yes (slight edge) |
| $P(\text{Sunny} \mid C_k)$ | $2/9 = 0.2222$ | $3/5 = 0.6000$ | No (strong) |
| $P(\text{Cool} \mid C_k)$ | $3/9 = 0.3333$ | $1/5 = 0.2000$ | Yes |
| $P(\text{High} \mid C_k)$ | $3/9 = 0.3333$ | $4/5 = 0.8000$ | No (very strong) |
| $P(\text{Strong} \mid C_k)$ | $3/9 = 0.3333$ | $3/5 = 0.6000$ | No |
| **Naive Bayes Score** | **0.00529** | **0.02057** | **No (3.9× higher)** |
| **Normalized Posterior** | **20.46%** | **79.54%** | **No** |
